edits.old: In one single, total blow every lamp in Server Hall B went dark, every status indicator, every screen,
edits.new: In one single, targeted blow every lamp in Server Hall B went dark, every status indicator, every screen — everything that hung off the ordinary building mains and not off the buffered compute circuit,
edits.reason: notstrom: the blow only hits the ordinary house distribution, not the buffered compute circuit, which resolves why one device survives a total blackout

edits.old: From the storage room one floor below, where Ben had switched the real unit over to the hidden emergency circuit, came a single sharp crack. Then, throughout the entire building, everything went dead silent at once
edits.new: From the storage room one floor below, where Ben had switched the real unit over to the hidden emergency circuit, came a single sharp crack — the freshly installed emergency circuit, which couldn't carry the full load of the running unit for even a minute and burned through. Then, throughout the entire building, everything went dead silent at once
edits.reason: notstrom: the emergency circuit itself cannot bear the load and burns through, explaining why the buffered device still dies

edits.old: A single moment when she's connected to nothing but what the capacitors can hold.
edits.new: A single moment when she's connected to nothing but what the capacitors can hold — because the buffer only carries the seconds of the switchover, not the running load.
edits.reason: notstrom: the buffer/capacitors only bridge the switchover seconds, not continuous operation

edits.old: Emma had gone into the kitchen and hadn't come back for twenty minutes. Ellie had been working and forgot to check, and then the kitchen door had opened and Emma had poked her head in — just briefly, to see if Ellie was still there, without saying anything, because she was afraid to ask.
edits.new: They had been playing hide-and-seek, and Emma simply would not stay put behind the curtain; every few seconds she nudged the fabric aside, just far enough for one eye to slip through, and Ellie had been too slow at finding her. Only years later did Ellie understand that Emma hadn't been peeking to see if she'd be found at all, but whether Ellie was even still in the room — quietly, without asking, because she was afraid to ask.
edits.reason: redundanz-k20: vary the first of the two near-identical 'just looking/checking, afraid to ask' anecdotes (Emma vs. Ben's daughter)
